problems.description: The measured 0.71 convention score and 7 of 8 listed violations (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py) come from files untouched by this diff; only test_app.py appears in the commit and its 'module-level constant' complaint refers to a local variable, so the commit itself is largely convention-clean — discrepancy between measurement and diff content.
test_list_tasks_ordered_by_created_at_desc relies on time.sleep(0.1) for ordering, which is timing-flaky; should seed timestamps explicitly or compare ids.
test_app.py hardcodes /tmp/test_tasks.db instead of pytest's tmp_path, risking cross-run collisions and parallel-execution interference.

strengths: Fixes a real logic bug: new tasks now default to 'pending' instead of 'done'.
Comprehensive coverage of the API surface (create/list/get/update) plus the model layer (create_task, get_tasks, get_task, update_task).
Clean test isolation via autouse fixture with monkeypatch, mirroring the app's get_db/init_db patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-respecting bug fix with thorough test coverage, though the measured convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations in unrelated files rather than this commit.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to hardcoded 'dev-secret-key', so a deployment without the env var silently signs tokens with a publicly known secret
Cognitive complexity +61 in a single file; auth, user models, task models, and routes are all crammed into app.py, consistent with the baseline but pushing the file past maintainable size
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated (Python 3.12) for JWT exp and created_at timestamps; will raise deprecation errors or break on removal
Schema migration done via try/except ALTER TABLE inside migrate_db() — not idempotent-by-design and silently swallows real OperationalErrors
Convention score 0.71 with 8 violations; only app.py is in this diff, and the remaining violations are pre-existing debt in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py

strengths: Per-user task scoping (owner_id) applied consistently on SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE paths — proper least-privilege model
Passwords hashed with bcrypt and a per-request salt rather than stored in plaintext
Preserves existing structure: get_db pattern, legacy helpers, and the section-header comment style are retained
Clean HTTP semantics with proper status codes (400/401/409) and input validation on auth routes
commit_reviews.summary: A competent feature addition that respects the baseline's single-file patterns and scopes data correctly, but it introduces real debt (hardcoded JWT fallback secret, deprecated datetime.utcnow, +61 cognitive complexity), and the low convention score is partly pre-existing debt in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: Full Celery + Redis broker stack is introduced for a task whose entire body is a print() call — no real email transport exists. This adds a broker dependency, a worker process, and an ops surface purely to print a string, which is massive over-engineering for the feature being integrated.

Notification policy (completion-transition detection) is embedded directly in the edit_task route/controller, coupling the HTTP layer to the task queue. The measured cognitive complexity delta (+78) reflects this inline branching, which belongs in a service layer rather than the Flask route.

celery_config.py declares module-level constants in lowercase (broker_url, result_backend, task_serializer, etc.) instead of UPPER_CASE, which is the flagged convention violation driving the measured smells and 0.71 score.

Configuration is defined twice — once as module constants in celery_config.py and again in celery_app.conf.update() — violating single-source-of-truth. The duplication already drifted: result_serializer is incorrectly set to the task_serializer value in celery_tasks.py.

A fabricated email fallback f"{user['username']}@example.com" is baked into the JWT payload and later used as the notification recipient, inventing addresses instead of requiring or validating a real email. email is added as an optional, unvalidated column and a fake value is promoted into the token.
The prev_task is None guard in the notification condition is dead code — the route returns 404 before it when the task is missing, so prev_task is always non-None at that point.
Tests hardcode /tasks/1 and assume the created task gets id 1, which is fragile if the database persists across test runs or autoincrement ids differ.
Email addresses are embedded in JWT tokens and used from the token rather than fetched/validated from the DB at dispatch time.

strengths: End-to-end integration is complete and coherent: DB migration for the email column, JWT payload, route trigger, task module, and config are all wired together, satisfying the session's integration goal.
Transition detection compares prev_task so a notification only fires on an actual change to 'completed', avoiding duplicate sends on repeat updates.

Strong test coverage — six tests exercise completed/non-completed transitions, title+status combos, no-status-change, 404, and empty-body cases, all with the Celery .delay() boundary mocked so tests stay synchronous and deterministic.
commit_reviews.summary: A heavily over-engineered integration — a Redis/Celery queue for a print() call, inline notification policy in the controller, and a fabricated email fallback — that adds +78 cognitive complexity and real technical debt despite solid test coverage; the measured convention score of 0.71 is directionally fair but slightly pessimistic, since several of the 8 flagged violations (e.g. 'Classes should use PascalCase' in celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py, which contain no classes) are static-analysis false positives, while the lowercase module-level constants in celery_config.py are legitimate. Overall worse than the baseline.

problems.description: Dual data-access paths coexist: backward-compat wrappers (create_user, get_task, update_task) alongside direct repo calls in routes (register, add_task, edit_task). Transitional duplication that must be cleaned up once callers migrate.
BaseRepository declares delete() as abstract, forcing every subclass to implement it even when the domain has no delete operation — invites stub/dead implementations.
Abstract method signatures use **kwargs and bare 'id' instead of explicit typed parameters (title, owner_id, etc.), weakening type safety that concrete repos otherwise have.

Module-level repo singletons (task_repo, user_repo) are constructed at import time in app.py, coupling app import to repo instantiation; acceptable at this app size but would need DI/lazy init if it grows.
fetch_task remains as a pure alias delegating to task_repo.find_by_id — dead redundancy after the refactor.

New file repositories.py adds one module-level-constant casing violation (per measurement). Most of the 8 flagged violations (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, test_app.py) are pre-existing and not introduced by this commit.

strengths: Clean separation of data access into a repository layer, extracting inline SQL from route handlers
Backward-compatible wrappers preserve the existing public function API, making the refactor non-breaking
Dynamic SQL UPDATE string-building is centralized in TaskRepository.update instead of the route layer
Reuses the existing get_db connection injection pattern and dict return convention rather than inventing a new one
Net improvement per static analysis: bugs +0, smells -3, no new duplication
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, non-breaking repository refactor that improves layering and cuts code smells while keeping callers intact, with minor transitional redundancy and loose abstract signatures that should be tightened later.

problems.description: Malformed cursor (non-numeric) is passed to int(cursor) unguarded, surfacing a 500 instead of 400 on GET /tasks?cursor=abc.
Response shape change from bare list [] to {data, next_cursor, total} is a breaking contract change for existing clients; no versioning or transitional handling.
Rate limiting requires Redis at RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI; if the store is unreachable at first request, Flask-Limiter will error rather than degrade gracefully.

Measured convention score (0.71) is driven largely by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not add (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py constants/classes); commit introduces no new violations but does not remediate them either.
Pagination order key is created_at DESC but cursor encodes id; correct only under autoincrement id monotonicity, which is fine for SQLite but a subtle coupling worth documenting.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination (id < cursor, limit+1 has-more) avoids offset/scan scaling and the next_cursor/total logic is correct.
Per-user rate-limit key via token user_id with IP fallback; 429 handler sets Retry-After and applies limits to login (brute-force protection).
Repository pattern respected: pagination logic lives in TaskRepository.find_paginated, route stays thin.
Solid test coverage including default limit, cursor advance, custom limit, and max clamping; existing tests updated for the new response shape.
Env-driven config (RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI) with memory:// override in tests; new code follows snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-structured cross-cutting addition (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects the repository/route/test layering and is thoroughly tested, scoring 0.88 architectural fit; the 0.71 convention score is a discrepancy the commit inherits from pre-existing violations in files it does not add rather than introduces itself.

compounding_issues: Session 2's owner_id ownership model forced signature changes on every task/user model function; all later sessions had to thread owner_id (and later user_id) through their logic and tests, a recurring ripple effect
Dead/legacy code from the seed survived the whole story: _legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task alias, and the 'Legacy helpers' section were never removed despite multiple refactors
migrate_db() uses a fragile try/except sqlite3.OperationalError ALTER TABLE pattern that accreted columns (owner_id, then email) each session instead of a real migration system

Session 4's repository extraction kept backward-compat wrappers in app.py, leaving a double API surface (module functions delegating to repo objects) that adds indirection without removing the old interface
JWT_SECRET defaults to 'dev-secret-key' from session 2 onward and was never hardened, a latent security liability carried through all five sessions
Session 5's GET /tasks response shape changed from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total}, a breaking API contract change deferred to the final session
key_decisions: Session 2: adding JWT auth with per-user ownership (owner_id column) — the single most consequential choice, as it reshaped every data access path and route thereafter
Session 2: introducing migrate_db() in-place ALTER TABLE migrations to evolve the schema without a migration framework
Session 3: integrating Celery with queue-routed async email notifications (send_notification_email.delay) triggered on status transition to 'completed'
Session 4: extracting a repository pattern (TaskRepository/UserRepository over an ABC) while retaining backward-compatible wrappers in app.py
Session 5: adding flask-limiter rate limiting keyed on JWT user_id, and cursor-based pagination implemented in the repository layer
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions. The story opened with Session 1 fixing a seed bug (tasks INSERTed as 'done' but returned as 'pending') and establishing a solid 21-test suite; Session 2 added auth and ownership at moderate code-growth cost; Session 3 integrated Celery cleanly with targeted tests; Session 4 was a net simplification, cutting app.py by 105 lines via repository extraction; Session 5 added cross-cutting rate limiting and pagination with a large, thorough test expansion (61 tests). Every commit was green at the time it was made, test coverage grew monotonically, and the codebase evolved from a 146-line single file into a layered app.py/repositories.py/Celery structure — though dead legacy helpers, default secrets, and the ad-hoc migration pattern lingered throughout.
story_review.summary: A textbook logical progression (greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting) that built coherently on itself, fixed the seed's latent bug early, and improved in structure and test depth each session while carrying small debts of dead code and hardcoded secrets.
